oh_pit_the.blurb: A small group of sandstone boulders inside Great Seal State Park, a short drive from Chillicothe in southwest Ohio. It holds 16 problems spread evenly from the easiest grades up through about V3, so it suits newer boulderers and anyone wanting a mellow afternoon. The blocks are not tall, but the lines are fun. The setting is wooded, lightly shaded and quiet, and you reach it on foot along a ridge trail that takes roughly three quarters of a mile. Expect natural sandstone of varying quality rather than a polished crag, and bring a pad for the uneven landings.

_expect.name: Pine Crest Trail Boulders aka Lakeside Boulders

oh_pine_crest_trail_boulders_aka_lakesid.blurb: Trailside sandstone boulders in Salt Fork State Park, in eastern Ohio, sitting beneath pines and overlooking the lake. This stretch has about 15 problems, mostly easy to moderate, running from VB-level warm-ups to a few V4 and V5 lines, which makes it a good spot for beginners and families of boulderers. The stone here is solid and well featured, noticeably sturdier than some other Ohio sandstone. A short walk along the loop trail from the lot gets you to the first blocks, so it works well for a quick session.

oh_4_crum_boulders.blurb: A cluster of boulders on the Pine Ridge ridgetop at Raven Rocks in Belmont County, eastern Ohio, just beyond the Balancing Rock. It holds 15 problems with a broad spread: a few easy V1 and V2 lines, a solid middle of V3 to V5, and a handful of hard ones up to a V9 at the top end. Most blocks are fairly low, though a few stand taller. The trail passes along one side of the group. Reaching the ridge takes a long, flat hike through pine forest, so this is a half-day outing rather than a quick stop.

oh_3_balancing_rock.blurb: A standout boulder perched on a pedestal beneath pines along the Pine Ridge ridgetop at Raven Rocks, Belmont County, eastern Ohio. It carries 15 problems, running from an easy V1 up through V7, with plenty in the V4 to V6 range, so it favors strong intermediate and advanced boulderers. One visitor ranks it among the best boulders in the state, and several lines would be highlights anywhere. It lies downhill from the Squirrel Stew boulder and is hard to miss. The walk in is a long flat hike, roughly 25 to 30 minutes, through forest.

oh_brady_s_bluff.blurb: A small, still-developing bouldering zone in the Tri-Valley Wildlife Area in central Ohio. Sandstone blocks sit along a steep hillside above a state route, with the best lines gathered in a northern ravine and a southern ravine nearby. Of the 15 climbs, nearly all are boulder problems, from VB and V0 up to a couple in the V7 to V8 range, plus one top-rope line around 5.11. The blocks are strung out, so expect real hiking on steep ground between problems. Several roadside pull-offs serve it; take care with traffic.

oh_d_katz_wall.blurb: One of the roped walls at the Marne Road crag near Newark in central Ohio, a short stroll right of the Warm-Up Wall. The 14 routes are mostly sport with three trad lines, spanning easy 5.5 and 5.6 climbs up through a solid group of 5.9s to several 5.11s. The easier lines are good for beginners or for setting a top rope for kids, while the technical slabs at the left end are tougher. Sandstone here ranges from firm to fragile, and the slabs and trad lines stay damp through winter and spring.

oh_greenwood_trail_boulders.blurb: Boulders strung beside the Greenwood Trail in the Marietta Unit of Wayne National Forest, southeast Ohio. The 14 problems split between a lower set and a smaller upper set reached from a different trailhead, and range from easy V1 and V2 through the V3 and V4 middle to a single V6. Expect dense woods, a trail hike of about 25 minutes to the lower group, and no cell service. Fall, winter and spring are the comfortable seasons, since summer gets hot and humid. Plenty of room remains for new lines.
